Key Takeaways

Oracle's credit default swaps widened again on Nov. 24 to a level ZeroHedge puts wider than Bear Stearns' in January 2008, a day after Jensen Huang's return as CEO sent Nvidia's stock up 32%.

Nvidia's backing doesn't settle Oracle's real problem, which is whether OpenAI can pay for the capacity Oracle is building for it.

Analysts expect Oracle's free cash flow to stay negative through fiscal 2028.

Hyperscaler swaps also hit record wides, which puts Meta and Amazon in the same conversation.

On Monday, investors cheered Jensen Huang's return as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) and sent its stock up 32%. By Tuesday, the credit market was back to worrying about Oracle (ORCL:NYSE).

Oracle's credit default swaps blew out again, and ZeroHedge says they're now wider than Bear Stearns' were in January 2008.

ZeroHedge also posted that hyperscaler swaps "blew out to record wide." Anyone holding Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) or Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) should notice, since both are spending more on AI capacity than their operations bring in.

What exactly happened

Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO on Nov. 23, and the companies Nvidia has propped up rallied hardest. CoreWeave and Nebius, neoclouds Nvidia holds stakes in, jumped 22% and 20% as traders bet that Huang would go back to using Nvidia's cash to backstop weaker AI players, Axios Markets reported.

That bet should help Oracle too. In an Oct. 20 note, TD Cowen said "NVIDIA is providing credit support" to Oracle, either through backstops or by leasing capacity directly and subleasing it, as Ed Zitron posted.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO and interim CEO until Huang's return, had stressed last week that Nvidia would be more selective about these investments. Huang's return seemed to put that backing back on the table, but Oracle's swaps widened anyway.

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on Oracle. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

OpenAI still has to pay the bill

Nvidia's help goes to Oracle's capacity. Oracle's credit is priced on whether OpenAI can pay for that capacity.

S&P has said OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle's backlog, which stood at $664 billion at the end of August. OpenAI posted a third-quarter operating loss of about $13.5 billion, based on The Wall Street Journal's figures, and its latest funding round has reached just $15 billion, half its original $30 billion target, per CNBC.

title: How Low Can Intuit Stock Go?

How Low Can Intuit Stock Go?

Intuit (INTU) stock fell 12.8% on November 20, 2026, the day after it cut its revenue forecast for fiscal 2027. Fears about AI have weighed on the shares, now 59.5% below their high of the past year. Buyers may hope the worst is over. That holds only if Intuit falls no further than the market in a sell-off, and TurboTax and Credit Karma keep growing. So how far has Intuit fallen when the whole market turned?

How Far Has Intuit Fallen In Past Sell-Offs?

Intuit's deepest fall on record was 75.3%, from December 1995 to April 1997. Its current 59.5% drop from its high of the past year is already deeper than any of its falls in a market sell-off since 2007. The largest of those was 44%. That was in the 2022 inflation shock, when the S&P 500 fell 24%. In a typical shock, though, Intuit has moved with the market. Across 15 shocks since 2007, it fell 15.5% on average, against 15.8% for the S&P 500.

Intuit stock fell 44% in the 2022 sell-off, close to twice the S&P 500's 24% fall. If Intuit is a large part of your savings, a second drop that deep would be hard to sit through. In a free 30-minute review, our partner advisory firm can show you ways to limit your loss if the stock falls further and to sell with a smaller tax bill. Book the free review.

From its low, Intuit took a median 1.7 months to get back to its high before the fall. Two recoveries took more than a year. The stock needed 19.2 months after 2022, and 14.6 months after the 2008-2009 financial crisis. So the sell-off that hit Intuit hardest was also the one it took longest to recover from.

Are Intuit's Sales And Profits Still Growing?

Yes, though sales are growing more slowly than a year ago. Intuit's revenue was $21.9 billion over the 12 months to October 31, 2026, up 12.8%. A year earlier, growth was 17.1%.

The Consumer segment, which holds TurboTax and Credit Karma, sold $8.58 billion in fiscal 2026. That was up 10.7%, after 14.8% growth the year before. Global Business Solutions, home to QuickBooks, grew 16.1%, about as fast as a year earlier.

Profit has held up better. Intuit's operating margin was 29.8% over the latest 12 months, up from 26.7% a year earlier. It was higher than at 38 of the 40 quarter-ends since fiscal Q2 2017. Intuit's debt was $7.71 billion at October 31, 2026, against $6.89 billion of cash and short-term investments.

Intuit Has Cut Its Sales Forecast Over Credit Karma

Credit Karma revenue grew 9% in fiscal Q1 2027, below management's own expectations. Management blamed higher interest rates and a faster-than-expected shift by consumers toward AI-powered experiences. So Intuit lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $23.2 billion at the midpoint, from $23.4 billion. It said the change was limited to Credit Karma.

The stock lagged the wider tech sector, though. XLK, the fund for the S&P 500's tech stocks, gained 9%.

All five companies on Trefis's peer list for Snowflake rose. They are Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Palantir. Oracle gained 12.3%, and Microsoft gained 1.6%. Palantir is also among the application software companies above. A related question is Did The Sell-Off Punish Salesforce For Slow Growth?

Where does Snowflake stock stand after the gain?

A rise this size is not rare for Snowflake. It had 10 rises at least this large in the prior year. The latest earlier move this large, up or down, was a 7.2% fall on November 5.

Over the past year, from the November 20, 2025 close to Monday's close, the stock gained 10.9%. The S&P 500 returned 12%, counting dividends. The past month was harder. Snowflake lost 16.6%, against a 5% loss for the S&P 500.

Monday's close of $271.27 sits well below $368.89, the highest close of the past year, set on October 9. For how far past falls went, see How Big Could Snowflake Stock's Next Fall Be?
